questions.q: During external OSINT for a PNPT engagement, which tool harvests employee names and email formats from search engines and public sources to seed a password-spray user list?
questions.why: theHarvester scrapes emails, subdomains, and names from public sources, ideal for building spray target lists.

questions.q: You breach an email address list and want to check which appeared in public credential dumps to reuse passwords. Which service is designed for that lookup?
questions.why: HIBP and dehashed map emails to breach data; dehashed exposes plaintext or hashed passwords for reuse checks.

questions.q: Which resource is best for enumerating subdomains of a target by mining Certificate Transparency logs during external recon?
questions.why: crt.sh queries CT logs, revealing subdomains from issued TLS certificates that DNS brute force may miss.

questions.q: An external pentest finds an Outlook Web Access portal. Which technique tests many discovered usernames against one common password to avoid lockouts?
questions.why: Spraying tries one password across many accounts, staying under lockout thresholds unlike per-account brute force.

questions.q: Before password spraying an on-prem AD-backed portal, why enumerate the domain account lockout policy first?
choices: To extract Kerberos tickets for offline cracking
To determine the SMB signing configuration
To identify which users are Domain Admins
To pace attempts under the lockout threshold and reset window and avoid locking users out
questions.why: Knowing the threshold and observation window lets you time sprays so no account crosses the lockout limit.

questions.q: On an internal network with no credentials, which Responder-based attack captures NetNTLM hashes by answering broadcast name-resolution requests?
questions.why: Responder poisons LLMNR and NBT-NS queries, coercing hosts to authenticate and leaking NetNTLMv2 hashes.

questions.q: You captured a NetNTLMv2 hash via LLMNR poisoning. What is the correct next step to obtain a usable plaintext credential?
choices: Crack it offline with hashcat mode 5600
questions.why: NetNTLMv2 is a challenge-response hash that cannot be passed; it must be cracked offline, hashcat mode 5600.

questions.q: Why can a captured NetNTLMv2 response not be used in a pass-the-hash attack?
choices: It only works against SMBv1 targets
It expires within 30 seconds of capture
It is encrypted with the domain controller Kerberos key
It is a salted challenge-response value, not the reusable NT hash
questions.why: Pass-the-hash needs the static NT hash; NetNTLMv2 mixes in a server challenge so it is not directly replayable.

questions.q: SMB relay converts a poisoned authentication into access on another host. What target configuration is required for the relay to succeed?
choices: The target must be a domain controller
SMB signing not required (disabled) on the relay target
The relayed user must be AS-REP roastable
SMB signing enforced on the relay target
questions.why: If SMB signing is not enforced, the relayed session is not integrity-checked, so ntlmrelayx can complete it.

questions.q: When running an SMB relay attack with Impacket ntlmrelayx, why must you disable Responder's SMB and HTTP servers?
choices: To prevent the domain controller from logging the event
To force NTLMv1 downgrade on the victim
To enable Kerberos armoring on the relay
So Responder does not answer the auth itself and instead lets ntlmrelayx relay it onward
questions.why: Responder and ntlmrelayx both bind SMB/HTTP; you disable Responder's so the coerced auth reaches the relay tool.

questions.q: A relayed account has local admin on the target. Which ntlmrelayx option dumps the local SAM hashes over the relayed session?
choices: The default action gathers SAM/secrets when the relayed user is local admin
questions.why: With admin over the relay, ntlmrelayx defaults to dumping the SAM database and local secrets from the target.

questions.q: Kerberoasting targets accounts with which attribute set, allowing any authenticated user to request a crackable service ticket?
choices: A servicePrincipalName (SPN) registered on the account
questions.why: Any account with an SPN can have a TGS requested; the ticket is encrypted with the service account NT hash.

questions.q: In a Kerberoasting attack, which part of the requested TGS is cracked offline to recover the service account password?
choices: The ticket portion encrypted with the service account's NT hash
The PAC signature from the KDC krbtgt key
The authenticator signed with the user's TGT session key
questions.why: The TGS is encrypted with the service account key, so cracking it (hashcat 13100) yields that account's password.

questions.q: Why are RC4-encrypted (etype 23) Kerberoast tickets generally preferred by attackers over AES tickets?
choices: RC4 hashes crack far faster because they derive directly from the NT hash
RC4 tickets bypass the account lockout policy
AES tickets are not encrypted with the service account key
AES tickets cannot be requested by normal users
questions.why: RC4 Kerberos keys equal the NT hash, so those tickets crack much faster than salted AES256 tickets.

questions.q: AS-REP roasting is possible against accounts that have which specific setting enabled?
questions.why: With preauth disabled, the KDC returns an AS-REP encrypted with the user's key that can be cracked offline.

questions.q: Which Impacket tool enumerates and requests AS-REP roastable hashes given a user list and domain?
questions.why: GetNPUsers.py finds accounts lacking preauth and outputs crackable AS-REP hashes (hashcat mode 18200).

questions.q: GetUserSPNs.py from Impacket is used in which attack against a domain?
questions.why: GetUserSPNs.py enumerates SPN accounts and requests their TGS tickets for offline Kerberoast cracking.

questions.q: You recovered an NT hash but not the plaintext. Which technique authenticates as that user without cracking it?
questions.why: Pass-the-hash uses the NT hash directly for NTLM authentication, no plaintext needed.

questions.q: Which command demonstrates pass-the-hash across a network using CrackMapExec with an NT hash?
questions.why: CrackMapExec accepts -H to supply the NT hash directly, spraying it across hosts to find local admin access.

questions.q: Overpass-the-hash (pass-the-key) uses an NT hash to accomplish what, moving from NTLM to Kerberos?
choices: Forge a golden ticket from the krbtgt hash
Request a Kerberos TGT using the hash as the RC4 key
Crack the hash into plaintext locally
Relay the hash to an LDAP server
questions.why: Overpass-the-hash feeds the NT hash as the RC4 Kerberos key to obtain a real TGT, then acts via Kerberos.

questions.q: On a compromised host with local admin, which mimikatz command dumps plaintext passwords and hashes from LSASS memory?
questions.why: sekurlsa::logonpasswords reads LSASS to extract cached credentials, NT hashes, and sometimes plaintext.

questions.q: Group Policy Preferences (GPP) passwords are a classic AD finding. Where and how are they recoverable?
choices: In LSASS as reversibly encrypted secrets
In the NTDS.dit encrypted with the boot key only
In SYSVOL Groups.xml, AES-encrypted with a Microsoft-published static key (cpassword)
In the registry SAM hive under LSA secrets
questions.why: GPP cpassword values in SYSVOL use a public static AES key, so any domain user can decrypt them.

questions.q: Which tool or command quickly finds and decrypts GPP cpassword values from a domain controller's SYSVOL share?
questions.why: Get-GPPPassword (PowerSploit) or gpp-decrypt locates Groups.xml cpassword and reverses the known AES key.

questions.q: BloodHound ingests AD data to reveal attack paths. Which component collects that data from the domain?
questions.why: SharpHound is the BloodHound collector, enumerating sessions, ACLs, group membership, and trusts into JSON.

questions.q: In BloodHound, which prebuilt query is most directly useful for planning privilege escalation from an owned user?
choices: Find computers with unconstrained delegation only
Map all GPO links in the domain
questions.why: Shortest path to Domain Admins highlights the fewest hops from your foothold to full domain compromise.

questions.q: BloodHound shows your user has WriteDACL over a group. How does this enable privilege escalation?
choices: You can request a golden ticket for that group
You can dump LSASS on the group's members
You can immediately DCSync the domain
You can modify the group's ACL to add yourself as a member
questions.why: WriteDACL lets you rewrite the object's DACL to grant AddMember, then join the group and inherit its rights.

questions.q: A BloodHound edge shows GenericAll over a user object. Which attack does this most directly enable?
choices: Reset the target user's password or set a targeted Kerberoast SPN
Perform an SMB relay to that user
questions.why: GenericAll grants full control, so you can force a password reset or add an SPN for targeted Kerberoasting.

questions.q: Token impersonation via incognito (or Meterpreter) abuses what to escalate on a compromised Windows host?
choices: Unconstrained delegation on the domain controller
Delegation/impersonation tokens left in memory by other logged-on users
questions.why: If a privileged user has a token on the box, impersonating it lets you act as that account, e.g., Domain Admin.

questions.q: You impersonate a Domain Admin token on a member server. What is a reliable next action to establish durable domain control?
choices: Relay the token to an SMB server
Add a controlled account to Domain Admins or DCSync the krbtgt hash
Run Responder to poison LLMNR again
questions.why: With DA rights you can DCSync secrets or add an account to a privileged group for persistent domain access.

questions.q: DCSync abuses which AD replication rights to pull password hashes without touching a domain controller's disk?
questions.why: DCSync uses the directory replication (GetChanges/GetChangesAll) rights to request secrets via MS-DRSR.

questions.q: Which Impacket command performs a DCSync-style dump of all domain hashes from NTDS given domain admin credentials?
questions.why: secretsdump.py -just-dc uses replication to extract every account's hash from the DC without a disk copy.

questions.q: A golden ticket forges a TGT for arbitrary access. Which secret must an attacker possess to create one?
questions.why: The krbtgt hash signs TGTs, so with it you can forge tickets for any user and group, including fake SIDs.

questions.q: How does a silver ticket differ from a golden ticket in an AD attack?
choices: A silver ticket is a cracked AS-REP hash
A silver ticket forges a TGS for one service using that service account's hash
A silver ticket requires domain admin replication rights
A silver ticket forges a TGT using the krbtgt hash
questions.why: A silver ticket is a forged service ticket signed with the service account key, granting access to that one service.

questions.q: Unconstrained delegation on a compromised server is dangerous because it allows an attacker to do what?
choices: Reset any user's password in the domain
Capture TGTs of any user who authenticates to the server, including a DC via coercion
Bypass SMB signing on all hosts
questions.why: Unconstrained delegation stores incoming users' TGTs in memory; coercing a DC yields the DC's TGT for takeover.

questions.q: After gaining a foothold on a dual-homed host, you need to reach a segmented internal subnet. Which technique routes your tools through the compromised host?
choices: Pivoting via SOCKS proxy / port forwarding (e.g., chisel, ssh -D, proxychains)
questions.why: A SOCKS proxy or port forward through the foothold lets you tunnel scans and exploits into the isolated subnet.

questions.q: You set up chisel to reach an internal subnet. What role does proxychains play in this pivot?
choices: It enumerates SPNs on the internal DC
It cracks the captured NetNTLM hashes
It forces command-line tools through the SOCKS proxy the tunnel exposes
questions.why: proxychains wraps tools like nmap or smbclient so their traffic exits through the pivot's SOCKS listener.

questions.q: During internal enumeration with valid creds, which CrackMapExec function checks where your user has local admin across many hosts at once?
choices: The (Pwn3d!) indicator when authenticating over SMB to each host
questions.why: CrackMapExec marks hosts with (Pwn3d!) when the supplied credential grants local admin, mapping lateral options.

questions.q: Which Impacket tool gives an interactive semi-shell over SMB using valid credentials or a hash without dropping a service binary noisily?
questions.why: wmiexec and smbexec run commands via WMI/SMB with creds or hashes, quieter than psexec's service install.

questions.q: You have a low-priv shell on Windows and check for privilege escalation. Which tool automates enumeration of misconfigurations and exploitable services?
questions.why: winPEAS surveys the host for unquoted paths, weak service perms, credentials, and other local privesc vectors.

questions.q: An unquoted service path with a writable intermediate directory lets an attacker do what for local privilege escalation?
choices: Request an AS-REP for the service account
Extract the krbtgt hash from the service
Place a malicious executable that Windows runs as the service's SYSTEM account
Relay the service's authentication to a DC
questions.why: Windows parses spaces in unquoted paths, so a planted binary in a writable segment runs with service privileges.

questions.q: Which registry-based Windows privesc looks for AlwaysInstallElevated set, allowing an MSI to run as SYSTEM?
choices: SMB signing disabled in the registry
HKLM and HKCU AlwaysInstallElevated both set to 1
questions.why: When both AlwaysInstallElevated keys are 1, any user can install a crafted MSI that executes as SYSTEM.

questions.q: Post-exploitation, you find a stored WiFi or scheduled task credential. What PNPT-appropriate action follows for cleanliness and value?
choices: Change the account's password to lock the client out
Document the credential and test its reuse across other systems and services
Ignore it because it is out of scope by default
Immediately delete the credential from the host
questions.why: Reused credentials often unlock lateral movement; you record findings and test reuse rather than destroy evidence.

questions.q: Which Windows post-exploitation location holds cached domain logon verifiers (DCC2) that can be extracted and cracked offline?
choices: The NTDS.dit only on the DC
The SECURITY registry hive (cached domain credentials)
questions.why: Cached domain credentials live in the SECURITY hive as DCC2 hashes, crackable offline (hashcat mode 2100).

questions.q: In the PNPT model, what deliverable must accompany the exam beyond obtaining domain admin in the lab?
choices: A recorded video of every command
questions.why: PNPT requires a full professional report; technical access alone does not pass without proper documentation.

questions.q: The PNPT exam uniquely includes which step after report submission?
choices: A peer code review of your scripts
An automated grading of exploit flags
A live 15-minute debrief presenting findings to assessors
questions.why: PNPT includes a live debrief where you present and defend your findings, mirroring a real client readout.

questions.q: A well-structured pentest report ranks findings by risk. Which pairing best drives that severity rating?
choices: The CVE publication date and vendor
The number of tools used to find it
Likelihood of exploitation combined with business impact
questions.why: Risk severity is derived from how likely a flaw is exploited and the damage it would cause to the business.

questions.q: In the report, which section is written for non-technical leadership to summarize risk posture and priorities?
questions.why: The executive summary conveys overall risk and top priorities in plain language for decision-makers.

questions.q: For each finding, why should a PNPT report include specific reproduction steps and evidence like command output or screenshots?
choices: To increase the page count for billing
So the client can verify, reproduce, and confirm remediation of the issue
To satisfy the exam's video requirement
To demonstrate which exploits are zero-days
questions.why: Reproducible steps and evidence let the client validate the flaw and later confirm the fix actually worked.

questions.q: When recommending remediation for LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning found on the internal network, what is the primary control to advise?
choices: Remove all SPNs from service accounts
Enable AS-REP preauth on all accounts
Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via Group Policy and enforce SMB signing
questions.why: Disabling the legacy name-resolution protocols removes the poisoning vector, and SMB signing blocks relay follow-on.

questions.q: On an external pentest you validate a successful password spray against OWA. What is the safest way to turn that into internal access?
choices: Kerberoast the account from the public internet
Run Responder against the mail server
Immediately DCSync the domain over the internet
Test the credential against exposed VPN or portal services that grant a foothold
questions.why: Valid domain creds are often reused on internet-facing VPN or portals, giving a legitimate path onto the internal network.
